---
title: "Automotive Trends"
subtitle: "Fifty years of U.S. EPA trends in fuel economy, horsepower, market share, and MY 2024 emissions"
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)
library(scales)

trends_df <- read_csv("data/processed/epa_trends_clean.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
epa24_df <- read_csv("data/processed/epa_clean.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

n_trends_rows <- nrow(trends_df)
n_epa24_rows <- nrow(epa24_df)
n_combined_epa <- n_trends_rows + n_epa24_rows

distinct_types <- c("Sedan/Wagon", "Car SUV", "Truck SUV", "Pickup", "Minivan/Van")
```

## Overview of EPA Automotive Trends Data (`N = `r comma(n_combined_epa)`` EPA Records)

To place recent **2022–2027** vehicles in historical context, this page analyzes two complementary U.S. Environmental Protection Agency datasets:

1. **Historical EPA Summary Trends (`epa_trends_clean.csv`, `n = `r comma(n_trends_rows)`` rows, MY 1975–2025):** Tracks fleetwide and segment-level real-world MPG, horsepower, inertia weight, footprint, and U.S. production share across 51 model years (model year 2025 values are marked preliminary by EPA and omit final production shares).
2. **Model Year 2024 Detailed Certification Data (`epa_clean.csv`, `n = `r comma(n_epa24_rows)`` vehicle configurations):** Captures model-level inertia weight, horsepower, fuel economy, and tailpipe $\text{CO}_2$ emissions across manufacturer compliance fleets.

---

## 1. Fifty Years of Real-World MPG and Horsepower (1975–2025)

How did automakers double fuel economy while simultaneously nearly doubling engine output? Below, we plot **Real-World MPG** and **Average Horsepower** from **1975 through preliminary 2025** across the overall U.S. fleet (`All`) and the five mutually exclusive EPA vehicle types (**`N = 306`** segment-year observations).

::: {.plot-container}
```{r}
#| label: fig-epa-mpg-hp-trends
#| fig-height: 6

focus_types <- c("All", distinct_types)

long_trends <- trends_df |>
  filter(vehicle_type %in% focus_types) |>
  select(year, is_preliminary, vehicle_type, mpg_real_world, horsepower, weight_lbs) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(mpg_real_world, horsepower),
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    metric_label = if_else(
      metric == "mpg_real_world",
      "Real-World Fuel Economy (MPG)",
      "Average Horsepower (hp)"
    ),
    prelim_note = if_else(is_preliminary, " (Preliminary)", ""),
    unit_str = if_else(metric == "mpg_real_world", " MPG", " hp"),
    hover_text = paste0(
      "<b>", year, prelim_note, " — ", vehicle_type, "</b><br>",
      metric_label, ": ", round(value, 1), unit_str, "<br>",
      "Avg Inertia Weight: ", comma(round(weight_lbs, 0)), " lbs"
    )
  )

n_trend_obs <- nrow(trends_df |> filter(vehicle_type %in% focus_types))

p_trends <- ggplot(
  long_trends,
  aes(x = year, y = value, color = vehicle_type, group = vehicle_type)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.85) +
  geom_point(aes(text = hover_text), size = 1.2, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ metric_label, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2") +
  labs(
    title = paste0(
      "U.S. Fleet Fuel Economy vs. Horsepower Over Time (N = ",
      n_trend_obs, " EPA Segment-Year Records, 1975-2025)"
    ),
    x = "Model Year",
    y = NULL,
    color = "Vehicle Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

ggplotly(p_trends, tooltip = "text") |>
  layout(
    legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.16),
    margin = list(b = 85)
  )
```
:::

**Patterns & Findings:**
Three distinct technological eras stand out in the `All` fleet line:
1. **1975–1985 Downsizing Era:** Following the first CAFE standards, fleetwide real-world efficiency jumped from **`13.1` to `21.3 MPG`** (`+63%`), achieved largely by cutting vehicle weight (`4,060` $\rightarrow$ `3,271 lbs`) and horsepower (`137` $\rightarrow$ `114 hp`).
2. **1985–2005 Horsepower & SUV Boom:** Fleetwide MPG stalled and slipped to **`19.9 MPG`** in 2005 because engine improvements were absorbed by rising weight (`4,059 lbs`) and surging output (**`209 hp`**).
3. **2005–2025 Electrification & Turbo Era:** Direct injection, multi-speed transmissions, hybrids, and EVs pushed **both** metrics to all-time highs—reaching **`28.1 MPG`** and **`264 hp`** fleetwide in preliminary 2025 (`335 hp` average for Pickups; `39.2 MPG` in 2024 for Car SUVs).

---

## 2. The Shift From Sedans to SUVs (U.S. Production Share, 1975–2024)

Because EPA's preliminary 2025 rows omit final production shares (`8` rows with `-` converted to `NA`), we examine verified production shares from **1975 through 2024** across all five mutually exclusive vehicle types (**`N = 250`** segment-year observations summing to `100%` each year).

::: {.plot-container}
```{r}
#| label: fig-production-share
#| fig-height: 5.2

share_df <- trends_df |>
  filter(vehicle_type %in% distinct_types, !is.na(production_share)) |>
  mutate(
    vehicle_type = factor(
      vehicle_type,
      levels = c("Truck SUV", "Car SUV", "Pickup", "Minivan/Van", "Sedan/Wagon")
    ),
    hover_text = paste0(
      "<b>", year, " — ", vehicle_type, "</b><br>",
      "Production Share: ", percent(production_share, accuracy = 0.1), "<br>",
      "Real-World MPG: ", round(mpg_real_world, 1), " MPG<br>",
      "Avg Horsepower: ", round(horsepower, 0), " hp"
    )
  )

n_share_obs <- nrow(share_df)

p_share <- ggplot(
  share_df,
  aes(x = year, y = production_share, fill = vehicle_type)
) +
  geom_area(alpha = 0.88, color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_point(aes(text = hover_text), alpha = 0, size = 0.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent()) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(
    title = paste0(
      "U.S. New-Vehicle Production Share by Body Type (N = ",
      n_share_obs, " EPA Records, 1975-2024)"
    ),
    x = "Model Year",
    y = "Share of U.S. New-Vehicle Production",
    fill = "Vehicle Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

ggplotly(p_share, tooltip = "text") |>
  layout(
    legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.18),
    margin = list(b = 85)
  )
```
:::

**Patterns & Findings:**
In **1975**, **Sedans and Wagons** accounted for **`80.6%`** of U.S. light-duty production while SUVs (`Truck SUV` + `Car SUV`) totaled just **`1.8%`**. By **2024**, those positions had completely inverted: **SUVs reached `60.2%`** of all new vehicles built (`49.6%` Truck SUVs + `10.6%` Car SUVs), **Pickups** held steady at **`14.1%`**, **Minivans/Vans** shrank to **`2.0%`**, and **Sedans/Wagons** fell to an all-time low of **`23.7%`**.

---

## 3. Model Year 2024 Inertia Weight vs. Tailpipe $\text{CO}_2$ Emissions

Using EPA's detailed **Model Year 2024** certification dataset (`epa_clean.csv`), **`1,975`** of `1,978` certified configurations report complete inertia weight and combined tailpipe greenhouse-gas emissions (`3` hydrogen fuel-cell configurations lacking standard GHG values are excluded). Measuring tailpipe **grams of $\text{CO}_2$ per mile** puts gasoline, diesel, hybrid, and zero-emission electric vehicles on the exact same physical scale.

::: {.plot-container}
```{r}
#| label: fig-epa24-weight-co2
#| fig-height: 5.8

epa24_plot <- epa24_df |>
  filter(!is.na(co2_gpm), !is.na(inertia_weight_lbs)) |>
  mutate(
    fuel_group = case_when(
      str_detect(fuel_type, regex("Electricity", ignore_case = TRUE)) & co2_gpm == 0 ~ "Battery Electric (0 g/mi)",
      str_detect(fuel_type, regex("Electricity", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Plug-In Hybrid",
      str_detect(fuel_type, regex("Diesel", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Diesel",
      TRUE ~ "Gasoline / Conventional Hybrid"
    ),
    hover_text = paste0(
      "<b>2024 ", make, " ", model, "</b><br>",
      "Manufacturer Group: ", manufacturer_group, "<br>",
      "Class: ", vehicle_class, "<br>",
      "Inertia Weight: ", comma(inertia_weight_lbs), " lbs<br>",
      "Tailpipe CO2: ", round(co2_gpm, 0), " g/mi<br>",
      "Label Combined Rating: ", mpg_combined,
      if_else(co2_gpm == 0, " MPGe", " MPG")
    )
  )

n_epa24_valid <- nrow(epa24_plot)

p_co2 <- ggplot(
  epa24_plot,
  aes(x = inertia_weight_lbs, y = co2_gpm, color = fuel_group, text = hover_text)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55, size = 1.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_comma(suffix = " lbs")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(suffix = " g/mi")) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Battery Electric (0 g/mi)" = "#1b9e77",
      "Plug-In Hybrid" = "#7570b3",
      "Gasoline / Conventional Hybrid" = "#d95f02",
      "Diesel" = "#666666"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = paste0(
      "Vehicle Inertia Weight vs. Tailpipe CO2 Emissions (N = ",
      comma(n_epa24_valid), " EPA Certified Models, MY 2024)"
    ),
    x = "EPA Base Level Inertia Weight (lbs)",
    y = "Combined Tailpipe CO2 Emissions (grams / mile)",
    color = "Fuel Category"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

ggplotly(p_co2, tooltip = "text") |>
  layout(
    legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.16),
    margin = list(b = 85)
  )
```
:::

**Patterns & Findings:**
Among **Gasoline / Conventional Hybrid** and **Diesel** vehicles, heavier curb weight translates steeply into higher tailpipe carbon output—climbing from roughly `120–180 g/mi` for `3,000–3,500 lb` compact hybrids up to `350–550+ g/mi` for `5,500–6,500 lb` full-size trucks and performance SUVs. Meanwhile, **Battery-Electric** models form a flat **`0 g/mi`** tailpipe floor stretching all the way to `7,000–8,500 lb` electric pickups and SUVs (such as Rivian and GM trucks), explaining how manufacturers with high EV shares—like **Rivian (`0 g/mi`)**, **Volvo (`133 g/mi`)**, **Kia (`135 g/mi`)**, and **Hyundai (`147 g/mi`)**—achieve dramatically lower fleet-average $\text{CO}_2$ than truck-heavy combustion lineups.
